big-bird-infinity-norm.summary: Lemma 5 claims that an ordinary softmax/ReLU transformer can approximate every network in an intermediate class, even in L∞. checks.claim: Every network in the modified hardmax/piecewise-linear class can be approximated arbitrarily accurately by an ordinary softmax/ReLU transformer, including at p=infinity.
checks.explanation: The modified class contains a unit jump, while every finite softmax/ReLU transformer is continuous. A continuous function has uniform approximation error at least $1/2$ across that jump, contradicting the $p=\infty$ case of Lemma 5. The cited approximation result covers finite $p$, which is enough for the main-text theorem’s stated range.
checks.demonstration:
Set the attention output weights to zero. A width-one feed-forward residual block with activation $\phi(t)=\mathbf1\{t>0\}$, bias $-1/2$ and a unit output weight realizes
$$\bar g_j(X)=X_j+e_1\mathbf1\{X_{j1}>1/2\}.$$
Here $e_1$ is the first coordinate vector. The same weights apply to every token, as required by the architecture. The activation has two constant pieces and therefore belongs to the cited modified class. Fix all input coordinates except $x=X_{11}$ in the interior of the input cube. Every finite softmax/ReLU transformer is continuous, so its affected output coordinate has a common limit $c$ from either side of $x=1/2$. The target's limits are $1/2$ and $3/2$, and therefore
$$\max\{|c-1/2|,|c-3/2|\}\ge\frac12.$$
For any threshold below $1/2$, the error exceeds that threshold on one side of the jump. Continuity within that side gives an open set of failing inputs with positive measure. Thus $d_\infty(g,\bar g)\ge1/2$ for both the supremum and essential-supremum interpretations. Taking $\varepsilon=1$ contradicts Lemma 5's bound of $\varepsilon/3$.
checks.repair: Restrict Lemma 5 to $1\le p<\infty$ and remove the $p=\infty$ endpoint from the appendix conclusion that depends on it. This is the range of the cited Yun et al. Lemma 9. The smoothing error can therefore vanish for finite $p$ while remaining bounded away from zero in the uniform norm. Restricting the lemma to the cited finite-$p$ range retains the range needed by the main-text Theorem 1. A uniform theorem for continuous targets would require a separate construction that controls the transition regions in the uniform norm.

addressed-ig002.summary: Bounded weights alone do not justify convergence of their expected logarithm.

checks.location: Theorem 1, PDF p.4; Appendix A.3, PDF p.10
checks.claim: Theorem 1 asserts Lk -> log p(x) whenever importance weights p(x,h)/q(h|x) are bounded; Appendix A step 3 infers expected-log convergence from the strong law.
checks.explanation: An upper bound on the weights does not control the logarithm near zero. Almost-sure convergence of sample means therefore need not imply convergence of their expected logarithms.
checks.demonstration: Let \(T\ge0\) have survival function \(\mathbb P(T>t)=1/\log(e+t)\), and set \(W=e^{-T}\). Then \(0<W\le1\) and \(\mu=\mathbb EW>0\). For independent copies, \[\frac1k\sum_iW_i\le e^{-\min_iT_i},\qquad-\log\left(\frac1k\sum_iW_i\right)\ge\min_iT_i.\] But \[\mathbb E\min_iT_i=\int_0^\infty\frac{dt}{[\log(e+t)]^k}=\infty\] for every fixed finite \(k\). Thus every \(\mathcal L_k=-\infty\), even though the sample means converge almost surely to \(\mu\). This is a valid importance-sampling model: take this law of \(T\) as the latent prior and proposal for observation \(x=1\), and set \(p(x=1\mid T)=e^{-T}\). The importance weight is exactly \(W\), and the evidence is \(\mu\).
checks.repair: Add uniform integrability of \(\log(k^{-1}\sum_iW_i)\). Strong consistency, continuity of the logarithm at \(\mu>0\), and uniform integrability then give convergence in expectation. A simple sufficient alternative is \(0<a\le W\le B<\infty\): every log average lies between \(\log a\) and \(\log B\), so dominated convergence applies. Filtering Variational Objectives, Proposition 1(b), gives the uniform-integrability repair; Hierarchical IWAE discusses the missing interchange condition in its convergence analysis.

trades-loss-domination.title: Theoretically Principled Trade-off between Robustness and Accuracy
trades-loss-domination.version: arXiv:1901.08573v3, 24 June 2019; ICML 2019 paper and supplement
trades-loss-domination.summary: Classification calibration says that choosing the wrong sign costs more than choosing the correct sign. It does not require that cost to be at least one. The second inequality of Theorem 3.1 needs precisely that stronger condition when it replaces a wrong-sign indicator by the loss. The smooth loss below meets the stated assumptions but charges only 1/2 at margin −1. On the permitted two-point input space, the resulting bound says that robust error one is at most 1/2. A non-increasing margin loss with φ(0)≥1 already satisfies the missing condition.

checks.location: Theorem3.1 surrogate upper bound for robust excess error; Statements/definitions physical pp3–6; full proof AppendixB.1 p20; published PMLR supplement p13
checks.claim: Theorem 3.1 upper-bounds robust excess error for any nonnegative classification-calibrated loss with φ(0)≥1, any measurable predictor and the stated instance space.
checks.explanation: Classification calibration requires a penalty for choosing the wrong sign, but it does not require that penalty to be at least one. The second inequality of Theorem 3.1 needs this stronger domination property when it bounds a boundary indicator by the loss. A nonnegative calibrated loss can satisfy $\phi(0)=1$ and still have $\phi(-1)=1/2$. Restoring the entire displayed chain also requires consistent treatment of zero scores.
checks.demonstration: Let $S(u)=0$ for $u\le0$, $S(u)=6u^5-15u^4+10u^3$ for $0<u<1$, and $S(u)=1$ for $u\ge1$. Define $\phi(t)=1-S(t)$ for $t\ge0$ and $\phi(t)=1/2+S(t+1)/2$ for $t<0$. This nonnegative twice continuously differentiable loss has $\phi(1)=0$, $\phi(0)=1$ and $\phi(-1)=1/2$. For $\eta=\Pr(Y=1\mid X)$, let $H(\eta)$ be the best conditional surrogate risk and $H^-(\eta)$ the best risk restricted to a wrong-sign score. They are $H(\eta)=\min(\eta,1-\eta)/2$ and $H^-(\eta)=\max(\eta,1-\eta)/2$, so it is classification-calibrated with $\psi(\theta)=\theta/2$. On the permitted space $\mathcal X=\{-1,1\}$, take uniform data, $Y=X$, $f(x)=x$, radius $2$ and $\lambda=1$. Surrogate excess risk and natural Bayes risk are zero, robust risk is one, and the largest boundary-surrogate value is $1/2$. The proposed bound becomes $1\le1/2$. Separately, take a singleton instance space with balanced random labels, $f\equiv0$, and normalized logistic loss $\phi(t)=\log(1+e^{-t})/\log2$. Under the printed $Yf(X)\le0$ convention, natural and robust risks are both $1$, while Bayes natural risk is $1/2$. The score zero minimizes the conditional logistic risk, so surrogate excess is zero. Boundary error is also zero because its definition requires $Yf(X)>0$. Thus the first, calibration-plus-boundary inequality would require $1/2\le0$. This is a separate failure of the first step, rather than another counterexample to the final surrogate bound displayed above.
checks.repair: Add $\phi(t)\ge1$ for every $t\le0$; a non-increasing loss with $\phi(0)\ge1$ is sufficient. Whenever a perturbation changes the sign or reaches a zero score, one product $f(x^{\prime})f(x)/\lambda$ is nonpositive, so its surrogate is at least one. Nonnegativity handles the complement of this event, and expectation gives the second inequality. For the entire chain under the paper’s convention that zero margins count as errors for both labels, also assume $\Pr(f(X)=0)=0$. Natural risk then coincides with ordinary classification risk, so the calibration inequality applies. A naturally correct nonzero score becomes adversarially incorrect exactly when a reachable score has nonpositive product with it. This proves the decomposition and the boundary bound together. Use a supremum if the maximum over the perturbation set is not attained.
checks.scope: The two-point construction concerns binary population theory with a deliberately non-monotone calibrated loss. The additional zero-score example concerns the printed tie convention. The corrected chain applies to non-increasing normalized margin losses and predictors with $\Pr(f(X)=0)=0$. These examples do not refute the released multiclass algorithm or its benchmark performance.
checks.whyItMatters: The theorem’s loss assumptions do not justify its second inequality on all permitted input spaces. Wrong-sign domination repairs that step; excluding zero scores on the data distribution also restores the first inequality under the stated error convention.

trades-loss-domination.paperSummary: TRADES studies how resistance to adversarial perturbations competes with ordinary prediction accuracy. trades-loss-domination.theoryRole: Theorem 3.1 helps justify replacing robust error, which is difficult to optimize directly, with a surrogate objective. The assumptions on that surrogate determine whether the same guarantee extends to other losses and input spaces.
